extracted.intended_audience: young people (especially young women), parents, and educators (Victorian-era readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and ethical guidance on reading, book-ownership, household arts, and personal conduct aimed primarily at young people (particularly young women) and their parents/educators. Emphasises choice and care of books, cultivation of useful skills, daily self-improvement, and charitable action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reading valueless books
rubrics_metrics.description: Life is short and the quiet hours of it few; we ought to waste none of them in reading valueless books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select reading matter deliberately; prioritise books of real value rather than ephemeral or trivial works. The lecture's stated purpose is to impress the importance of choosing worthwhile books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical quality of books
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuable books should, in a civilized country, be within the reach of every one, printed in excellent form, for a just price; but not in any vile, vulgar, or, by reason of smallness of type, physically injurious form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books needed for life should be clearly printed, on the best paper, and strongly bound; avoid ill-printed or loosely and wretchedly-stitched books even if poor—invest in legible type, good paper, and stout leather binding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a restricted, serviceable, steadily-growing library
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain as soon as you can, by the severest economy, a restricted, serviceable, and steadily—however slowly—increasing, series of books for use through life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build a small curated collection rather than amassing many worthless volumes. Treat the personal library as an important household possession (each volume 'having its assigned place').

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach careful handling of books
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the earliest and strictest lessons to the children of the house being how to turn the pages of their own literary possessions lightly and deliberately, with no chance of tearing or dog’s ears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instil habits of gentle use and care for books from childhood; display and store books respectfully (like statues in niches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-examination and daily improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The first duty of young people is to be delighted and delightful; but they are to be in the deepest sense solemn days... find out what you are now. Do not think vaguely about it; take pen and paper, and write down as accurate a description of yourself as you can, with the date to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep disciplined daily reflection: assess strengths and faults, resolve to improve a little each day, and record progress concretely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the two chief faults: Idleness and Cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: However good you may be, you have faults; but there are only two that are of real consequence,—Idleness and Cruelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make work (especially morning work) a habit and cultivate mercy; the text emphasises 'Work while you have light' and 'Be merciful while you have mercy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use morning (daylight) for work
rubrics_metrics.description: Work while you have light; especially while you have the light of morning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the day to use morning hours for productive and formative activity—morning has a special moral/psychological value as a time of solemnity and formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice arts for accuracy and service, not effect
rubrics_metrics.description: In music... Get your voice disciplined and clear, and think only of accuracy; never of effect or expression: if you have any soul worth expressing, it will show itself in your singing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train in arts (music, drawing) to be practically useful and communicative: music should sustain concerted parts reliably; drawing should set down the right shape to explain character to others; avoid showy or merely pretty work made for praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate useful domestic skills and teach them to others
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve to do every day some that is useful in the vulgar sense. Learn first thoroughly the economy of the kitchen; the good and bad qualities of every common article of food, and the simplest and best modes of their preparation: when you have time, go and help in the cooking of poorer families, and show them how to make as much of everything as possible, and how to make little, nice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical competence in household economy is moral work: teach it to poorer families, encourage tidiness, and use small ministries (like saying grace) as present religious practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make and provide useful clothing for the poor
rubrics_metrics.description: Let a certain part of your day... be set apart for making strong and pretty dresses for the poor. Learn the sound qualities of all useful stuffs, and make everything of the best you can get, whatever its price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn materials and tailoring; if quality goods are unavailable, buy raw material and organise local spinning/weaving; sew robustly and embellish moderately; accumulate garments to give when need arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active kindness; avoid complacent theological excuses for cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless you are deliberately kind to every creature, you will often be cruel to many... through the subtle encouragement of your selfishness by the religious doctrine that all which we now suppose to be evil will be brought to a good end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let abstract doctrines (e.g., 'Providence will make all right') excuse inaction; respond imaginatively to suffering and prevent avoidable harms rather than passively hope for ultimate ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on Providence to remedy practical mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: You do not expect Providence to make a carelessly prepared dish palatable; neither if, through years of folly, you misguide your own life, need you expect Divine interference to bring round everything at last for the best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take responsibility for consequences; use common sense and discretion to prevent and remedy harms instead of assuming divine correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gratitude should not be a form of pride or superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: If you belong to the middle or upper classes... you are probably gentle and grateful, and in the habit of every day thanking God for these things. But why do you thank Him? Is the essential meaning of your thanksgiving... 'Lord, I thank Thee that I am not as other girls are'?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflect on social position critically; avoid thankfulness that expresses contempt for others or complacency; cultivate compassion and just attitudes toward those less fortunate.

rubrics_metrics.name: True joy and religion expressed in justice, peace, and readiness to give
rubrics_metrics.description: The Kingdom of God means,—'not meat and drink, but justice, peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost'... such joy is not by any means, necessarily, in going to church, or in singing hymns; but may be joy in a dance, or joy in a jest, or joy in anything you have deserved to possess, or that you are willing to give.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value joyful moral life expressed in just acts and generosity rather than merely formal religious observance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charity should be humble, not performative
rubrics_metrics.description: All these professional pieties (except so far as distinction or association may be necessary for effectiveness of work) are in their spirit wrong, and in practice merely plaster the sores of disease that ought never to have been permitted to exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ostentatious or performative charity (e.g., public Sisters of Charity as status); practise steady, cheerful, effective kindness without veiled or voluble declaration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should be valued for its intrinsic worth, not only for social advancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents... seek 'the education befitting such and such a station in life'—they never seek, as far as I can make out, an education good in itself. It never seems to occur to the parents that there may be an education which, in itself, is advancement in Life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for education that furthers real moral and intellectual formation rather than merely training for social display or position; treat education itself as an end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid seeking advancement defined only as conspicuousness or applause
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Advancement in life' means becoming conspicuous in life; obtaining a position which shall be acknowledged by others... the gratification of our thirst for applause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of motives: prefer genuine achievement and character formation to the mere pursuit of reputation and applause; distinguish between making money and making known you have made it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be modest about claims to special divine insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Be quite sure of one thing... you have not been singled out, by the God who made you, from all the other girls in the world, to be especially informed respecting His own nature and character... if you care to behave with modesty or propriety, you had better be silent about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate theological modesty: do not assume special revelation or superior spiritual insight because of education, dress, or position.
